note: Per-EVIDENCE-BRANCH capability CONTRACT, enforced by scanner/tests/test_claim_discipline.py. fact_capable/clean_capable are SEPARATE claims describing what is TRUE TODAY. target_fact_capable/target_clean_capable are what the branch MUST become — this registry is a ladder, not a ceiling. Any gap between current and target REQUIRES `blocking_work`: the concrete engineering that closes it. A gap without blocking work fails the enforcement test, so a capability can never be quietly abandoned by downgrading the claim; the claim stays, and the system is built up to meet it. Downgrading a TARGET requires an explicit `target_downgrade_rationale` stating why the capability is not achievable at all. `evidence_surface` is a CLOSED type (response_headers | response_body | transport | tls_handshake | service_response | artifact | composite | live_capture) — rules key off the declared type, never off the branch name, so a future body-derived branch cannot escape them by being called something else. `implementation_refs` point at the code that realises the branch; the enforcement test checks the referenced file and symbol actually exist. `control_requirements` is the CLOSED-vocabulary list of standing capability controls (gates / VIGIL-owned captures / instrumentation / primary-artifact parses) a branch depends on to reach its declared capability — distinct from `preconditions`, which admission evaluates per observation; for a LEAD-only branch it names the MISSING controls that `blocking_work` closes. `oracle_version` names the OracleKind whose deterministic decision procedure adjudicates a FACT on this branch — the FACT certificate binds verify.oracle_version(kind) at mint so a verifier re-runs the SAME procedure — and is EMPTY for a LEAD-only branch, which no VIGIL oracle adjudicates yet (that is its blocking_work). The manifest validator (integration/vigil_integration/live/tool_manifest.py:validate_branch_registry) enforces both columns: fact_capable ⇒ a named oracle_version, LEAD-only ⇒ none. WHAT A CLEAN ACTUALLY CARRIES, and it is much less than a FACT: oracle_adapter.certify_admitted mints a signed, offline-re-verifiable evidence certificate ONLY for a FACT verdict; every other admitted verdict, CLEAN included, is returned as an AdapterResult(status='lead', outcome='clean') with NO signature, NO context digest and NO trust root. A CLEAN therefore has no cryptographic integrity at all - its only integrity is provenance-by-custody (it is whatever the process that produced it says it is), plus the fact that its deterministic predicate re-runs over the RETAINED capture. Nothing downstream can detect a CLEAN that was altered, reordered or invented after the run. This is true of EVERY clean_capable branch in this registry and must be said wherever a CLEAN is presented to an operator or a client.

branches.evidence: the outcome of a single bounded handshake in which VIGIL offered ONLY one deprecated protocol version (TLS1.0, then TLS1.1) to the scope-gated endpoint: either the negotiated version the endpoint AGREED to, or the alert the endpoint sent back on the established TCP channel - together with the peer_tls_session witness stamped into that retained capture from the run's OTHER captures of the same endpoint, which records whether VIGIL completed a full TLS handshake with this peer at some other version. The proposer tool's rows are never read; VIGIL performs the restricted ClientHello itself through the same audited gate as verify.reachability.
branches.limitation: The FACT is existential and exact, and is UNCHANGED: this endpoint completed a handshake at the deprecated version VIGIL offered. THE CLEAN IS WITHDRAWN. Until 2026-09-27 this branch was declared clean_capable and a peer alert(70) protocol_version on an established channel, corroborated by a peer_tls_session witness, cleared the endpoint for that version. That was WRONG, and a red-pen reproduced it end to end: the witness handshake and the refusal happen on TWO DIFFERENT TCP CONNECTIONS, and nothing in the retained evidence binds those two connections to the SAME PEER. Any L4 fan-out breaks it - a Kubernetes Service with more than one pod, an haproxy/nginx TCP pool, an L4 VIP, or a DNS A-record pool mid-rollout. One connection is answered by a backend whose minimum is TLS1.1 (a genuine alert(70)) and the next by a backend that speaks TLS1.0, so VIGIL retains a real refusal beside a real completed session and reports CLEAN for a version the endpoint DOES accept. Worse, the result is not detectable as a self-contradiction: minimum_version TLS1.1 is a legal configuration, so 'refused at TLS1.0, completed at TLS1.1' is internally consistent, and every guard in the predicate holds individually. The limit is IRREDUCIBLE with what TLS gives the refused leg: the COMPLETED leg retains spki_sha256, so key identity is available there, but the refusing peer sends the alert IN PLACE OF the ServerHello and presents no certificate, no server random and no session identifier - there is no material on the refused side to bind against. Repeating the probe k times would only make the claim probabilistic, which the oracle doctrine forbids. So a protocol refusal is now INCONCLUSIVE, always. THE GUARDS ARE KEPT AND STILL RUN: the closed singleton rejection vocabulary (tls_breadth.VERSION_REJECTION_REASONS), the channel_established precondition, and the peer_tls_session witness that closed the bare-alert(70) hole (a socket that is not a TLS service but answers every ClientHello with the same seven-byte alert(70) record). They are the right guards if this class is ever revived, they are mutation-defended sub-condition by sub-condition, and the round-robin pool is pinned as a permanent negative control in integration/tests/test_tls_breadth.py. Unchanged under-reporting: a server that refuses the version with a non-conforming alert, and a server that speaks ONLY the version being refused, were already INCONCLUSIVE. SSLv2/SSLv3 are outside the probe set because modern OpenSSL cannot offer them, so their absence is untested rather than clean.
branches.blocking_work: CLEAN requires a means of binding PEER IDENTITY ACROSS TWO CONNECTIONS THAT THE REFUSED LEG CAN ITSELF SUPPLY. That is the whole gap, and none of the material currently retained closes it: the refused leg carries only the alert, so spki_sha256 (which the completed leg does retain) has nothing to bind to. Concretely, one of: (1) an identifier the REFUSING peer emits - a TLS extension, or an out-of-band attestation the endpoint serves, that names the same key or instance the completed handshake authenticated. No such identifier exists in TLS 1.2 or 1.3 today, so this route is a protocol or deployment change, not code; or (2) narrowing the claim's SUBJECT from 'this endpoint' to 'the peer that answered THIS connection', which needs the refusal and a corroborating completed session on ONE TCP connection - not achievable with alert(70), which is fatal and terminates the connection it appears on. EXPLICITLY NOT ROUTES: repeating the probe k times and requiring k refusals (that makes the claim probabilistic, which the oracle doctrine forbids); and an operator-declared 'this endpoint is a single peer' flag carried in the charter (that is a DECLARATION, not a proof - it could at best support a conditional statement scoped to the declaration, and must never be rendered as a CLEAN).

branches.limitation: Scoped to the suites the LOCAL OpenSSL build can actually put in a ClientHello. Modern OpenSSL has removed RC4, single-DES, 3DES and the export suites from its default provider, so a large part of the vocabulary is not offerable (11 of the 29 names are offerable on the build this repo tests against) and the rest is UNTESTED rather than absent from the server. Because of that, and because handshake_failure(40) does not say whether the cipher or something else was the obstacle, a refusal here is INCONCLUSIVE: this branch may not assert that an endpoint supports no weak suite. An empty offerable set makes the probe a no-op (SKIPPED), not a negative result - and that no-op still goes through the audited gate, so 'the gate refused' and 'we were authorised and had nothing to offer' stay distinguishable in the evidence. Also scoped to TLS1.2: the probe pins the negotiated version at exactly TLS1.2 at both ends, because tls_weakness_oracle fires on a deprecated VERSION before it inspects the suite, so without the floor a FACT filed under this branch could have been adjudicated by the version predicate rather than by the cipher. The cost is that an endpoint whose maximum is TLS1.0 or TLS1.1 is NOT weak-cipher tested here (the probe gets a version refusal and the re-drive is SKIPPED, never CLEAN); that endpoint's deprecated protocol is already a FACT on tls_weakness.deprecated_protocol_offer.
